6.2 — Ground Checks: No Infinite Jumps

Your jump is limited, and the limit has a hole in it. The budget — jumpsRemaining, maxJumps, one refill per landing — is right. What is wrong is how it learns you are on the ground: a collision callback that fires when something tagged Ground touches you. That callback never tells you when you leave, so stepping off a ledge leaves you a full jump you did not earn. And it only answers for surfaces somebody remembered to tag. Today you replace the ear with a question: a ray, cast every frame from the player's feet, filtered to one layer — and then use it to charge one jump for walking off.

Search terms for this lesson“in unity how to check if the player is on the ground, how to raycast downward with physics2d.raycast, how to use a layermask to find ground, how to stop infinite jumping”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

Your file already limits the jump: a jumpsRemaining count, a maxJumps ceiling, and a refill that fires when a collision callback reports something tagged Ground. It works — and it has two holes you can feel. Walk off a ledge and your budget is still full, because nothing ever told you that you left. And every surface that should count has to be tagged by hand, so one forgotten object is a floor that silently is not ground. The count is right; the way it learns is wrong. Three changes: ask a ray instead of waiting for a callback, charge one jump when you leave without jumping, and move the answer from a name to a category.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Ask the ground a question once per frameA Physics2D.Raycast() from an empty child at the player's feet, pointed down, a short distance, and filtered to one layer. It runs in Update() because it answers a question about now — unlike the lookups in Start(), which answer questions about setup.Read: the Physics2D.Raycast() row of the quick reference, and the void Update() row from 1.4
  2. Write the budget you already have, in the frame loopjumpsRemaining and maxJumps keep their names and their meaning; they just get written in Update() — refilled while the ray hits, spent when you jump — instead of inside a collision callback. The collision method comes out.Read: the field declarations from 1.3
  3. Spend one when the key goes downThe jump condition from 6.1 with one term added, then jumpsRemaining -= 1 right after the jump. The gate decides; the decrement records. Both lines, in that order.Read: the jump you wrote in 6.1
  4. write this partRead: the if (isGrounded) branch you are about to write, and 6.1's rule that a value which does not change is written where it is decided
  5. Charge yourself one for walking offThe same budget, written from the other side: if the ray misses and the count is still full, then nobody jumped — you fell. A full budget in mid-air is the definition of "I walked off", and it needs no history to detect.Read: the else if you have been writing since 1.6, and the budget from part two
  6. Say which surfaces count as groundThe Ground layer, and the two objects you put in it. Because a mask filters by category rather than by name, the cave mouth joins the floor without a second line of code — and anything you forget to assign silently does not count.Read: the layer list in Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers
  7. Watch the number while you build, then take the instrument outA print() in Start() reports the budget you begin with, and the ray drawn in the Scene view shows what the check can see. Both are instruments for one afternoon, not features.Read: print() from 1.3

Most of those seven parts are work you have already done: the two ints are already in your file, the jump is 6.1, an if/else if is 1.6, and a layer is a name you type once. The new idea is narrow and worth saying out loud — a check that only listens cannot answer a question about now. A collision callback fires on the frame something changes; "am I standing on something?" is a question whose answer can change while nothing happens at all. The second new idea is the mirror image: once you can ask that question every frame, the ledge stops being a free jump, because a full budget in the air is proof that you walked off.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Stop the free jump off a ledge" cannot be looked up. "Cast a ray downward and report whether it hit" can.

Your turn

Your budget is refilled by asking a question every frame, not by waiting for a message from the physics engine. Name one moment where asking is the only way to know, and what the player sees when a check that only listens gets it wrong.

maxJumps is 1. Before you change it to 2, say what else in this lesson would have to be true for a second jump to actually be a second jump — and what the walk-off rule does to a player carrying two.

In the Editor ~15 min
  1. Project window → open Assets/_Scenes/Platformer.unity, then Game view → press Play and try both holes. Walk off a ledge and press the jump key while falling: you jump, because the budget has been full since your last landing and nothing ever spent it. Then jump onto the Cave Exit at the mouth of the cave and press it again: you get nothing, because that object is solid but untagged, so the callback never heard it. One rule, two failures, and the Console says nothing either time.
  2. Project window → Assets/Prefabs/Player, then Hierarchy → right-click the Player root and Create Empty. Rename it GroundCheck, then Inspector → Transform → Position set it to 0, -0.5, 0: the bottom of the collider, in the player's own coordinates. This is the point the ray will start from.
  3. Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers → Layers → take the first empty user slot (index 8) and name it Ground. Read the list while you are in there: the project ships with Layer 1, Layer 2, Layer 3 — placeholders nobody ever renamed — and no Ground layer at all.
  4. Hierarchy → Grid → Collision → Inspector → Layer set it to Ground. Then Hierarchy → Cave Exit → Inspector → Layer: also Ground. Nothing else changes, and nothing is tagged.
  5. Hierarchy → the Player → Inspector → Player Controller: drag the GroundCheck child into the Ground Check slot, leave Ground Distance at 0.2, and open the Ground Mask dropdown to tick Ground and nothing else.
  6. Game view → press Play and look at the Scene view: a short red line hangs under the player's feet while your code runs. 7.2 finishes the rest of the layer list, but the one layer your check needs exists after this step.
The cave mouth used to be a trap. The layer is why it is not. In the tag version of this check, Cave Exit is solid and untagged, so landing on it gave nothing back and the player would tell you the game was broken. A mask asks "is this in the category?" instead of "is this that one named thing?" — so assigning the layer fixes the cave mouth without touching a script and without tagging anything else. What it does not fix: anything you forget to assign is silently not ground, and nothing warns you.

Socratic: Asking Versus Being Told

  1. Which spot in your cave is a poor stand-in for your whole body under one exact point — and what does the player experience there?
  2. Why is "a full budget while airborne" the same fact as "I walked off"? And what would the rule have to remember if you wrote it the other way?
  3. maxJumps is 1 today. If you changed it to 2 right now, would you get a double jump? Name every line that would have to be true for the second jump to actually work — including what the walk-off rule does to a player carrying two.
In the Code ~20 min

There are three common ways to answer "am I standing on something?". Your file uses the first row right now, and the two failures you found in the editor are the two holes that row has. Today you move to the third. Read all three — the difference is in when each one knows, and what it can tell you when it does.

TechniqueWhen it knowsWhat it can tell youWhere it lies to you
OnCollisionEnter2D() plus CompareTag() On the frame contact begins — a message from the engine. That you touched something, and what that something is named. Nothing fires when you leave, so the budget stays full until you land again; and every new surface needs the tag by hand.
OnTriggerEnter2D() on a small child under your feet On the frame the child's trigger overlaps something. That a particular point on your body is touching something. The child has to be placed by hand, and a trigger that starts inside a collider reports it forever.
Physics2D.Raycast() every frame Whenever you ask — every frame, for as long as you want. Whether something is under one exact point, how far away it is, and what it is. An infinitely thin line: a pixel of your foot over a ledge reports air. It also needs a LayerMask to filter what it may notice.

The third row is what you build today, and it is what makes the walk-off rule possible: a callback only fires when something changes, and "did I leave the ground this frame?" is a question you can only ask.

In the CodeGuided build

The question this answers“in unity how to check if the player is on the ground, how to raycast downward with physics2d.raycast, how to use a layermask to find ground, how to stop jumping after walking off a ledge”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. One new method, two new fields for it to read, and four blocks that move the budget out of a collision callback and into the frame loop. Everything is a shape from earlier in the course except the ray itself and the charge for walking off — and one line is yours: the refill.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Give the check somewhere to stand, and a distance to look

Three fields in the class body, beside jumpForce from 6.1. The child they point at is the one you made in the editor half.

    [SerializeField] Transform groundCheck;
    [SerializeField] float groundDistance = 0.2f;
    [SerializeField] LayerMask groundMask;

    bool isGrounded;
  1. 1The empty child at the player's feet. Declared as a Transform because that is all a ray needs — a position and a direction. [SerializeField] because it is a reference you wire in the Inspector, exactly like the prefab and spawn point slots on the turret.Why not transform.position? Because the player's centre is not the player's feet. A ray from the middle of the body starts inside the floor it is standing on, or misses it entirely, depending on the sprite's pivot. A named child is a decision you can see and move.
  2. 2How far below the feet the ray is allowed to look. A fifth of a unit: long enough to reach the floor when the body settles, short enough that the player is not "grounded" while visibly floating.
  3. 3What the ray is allowed to notice. An int in a mask's clothing: each tick in the Inspector sets one bit. Point it at the Ground layer and the ray ignores coins, enemies and the backdrop without a single if.A mask that names a layer nobody made goes empty, and empty means "notice nothing". Then the ray never hits, isGrounded is always false, and the player jumps in mid-air forever — the exact bug this lesson is supposed to cure, reached by a different road. When the check "does not work", read this field before you read your logic.
  4. 5The answer, remembered for one frame. A field rather than a local because three different blocks in Update() ask the same question and must get the same answer.

Step 2Ask the question in a method of its own

Beside Jump(). One line of work, one line of signature — and the name is what lets 6.3 and 7.2 point at it.

    void CheckGround()
    {
        isGrounded = Physics2D.Raycast(groundCheck.position, Vector2.down, groundDistance, groundMask);
    }
  1. 1A method with no parameters and no return value: it writes the field instead of handing an answer back. That is the same shape as Jump(), which writes to the body.One question, one place. 6.3 adds a coyote window that reads this field, and 7.2 changes what sits in the mask. Neither has to find the ray again if the ray lives here.
  2. 3**Read the call as a sentence: cast a ray from here, downward, this far, noticing only these layers.** It returns a RaycastHit2D, which you can treat as a bool — true when it hit something.The return value is more than a yes. RaycastHit2D also carries the point it struck, the distance, and the collider — the ground check only needs the "did it hit", and the other fields are there the day you need to know what you landed on. That is the whole difference from a collision callback: the ray is a question, and you choose when to ask it.

Step 3Make the invisible ray visible

A gizmo. It draws in the Scene view, it costs nothing at runtime, and it is how you find out your child is two units above the floor.

    void OnDrawGizmos()
    {
        if (groundCheck == null) { return; }
        Gizmos.color = Color.red;
        Gizmos.DrawLine(groundCheck.position, groundCheck.position + Vector3.down * groundDistance);
    }
  1. 1A Unity message that runs in the editor, outside Play mode. It draws shapes into the Scene view and does nothing in the built game.Check for a null first. Before the slot is wired, groundCheck is null and reading .position throws. A one-line guard keeps the editor quiet while the half-built script sits on the Player.
  2. 3Leave without drawing when there is nothing to draw from. return in a void method ends it on the spot — the early exit you first saw in UpdateAnimation() and again in the turret's guard.
  3. 4Set the drawing colour before you draw. Color.red is a built-in constant, the same idea as Vector2.down.
  4. 5A line from the feet to the end of the ray. Vector3.down * groundDistance is the same direction-and-length the ray uses, which is why the gizmo is worth writing: the two must agree.

Step 4Keep the budget. Change where it is written

These two fields are already in your file from the day you built the jump limit — keep their names and their values. What moves is the refill: it comes out of the collision callback and into the frame loop.

    int jumpsRemaining;
    int maxJumps = 1;

            jumpsRemaining = maxJumps;
            print(jumpsRemaining);
  1. 1How many jumps are left right now. No initializer: a field of type int starts at 0, and Start() fills it. Nothing here changes today.Why not just start it at 1? Because a value that is set in two places is a value you can forget to reset in one of them. Give it one source of truth — maxJumps — and set it from that everywhere.
  2. 2How many jumps you are allowed between landings. 1 today; 2 is a double jump, and that is the whole of 6.4 — one number, plus a pickup that changes it.The limit lives in its own field, not in the condition. Written as jumpsRemaining >= 1 the 1 is hidden inside the gate; written as maxJumps the number has a name you can find, change and explain.
  3. 4Start on the floor with a full budget. In the else branch of Start() — the platformer branch from 6.1 — beside the gravity line. If it is already there, leave it: the first frame of the cave is a special case, and this is where special cases go.This is the same sentence as the landing, said once at the beginning. A field that gets its value from another field is telling you where the real number lives.
  4. 5An instrument, not a feature. One line in the Console at the start of the cave. Delete it once the number is right — or leave it and be able to say why.Not a Debug.LogError(). This is not a failure; the game is working. A red line in the Console means "something is wrong", and spending that colour on a number you are watching trains you to ignore it.

Step 5Spend it, refill it, and charge for the fall

In Update(), the platformer branch — the else where linearVelocityX is set. Four blocks, in this order, and the order is the lesson.

            CheckGround();

            if (isGrounded)
            {
________________
            }
            else if (jumpsRemaining == maxJumps)
            {
                jumpsRemaining -= 1;
            }

            if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.J) && jumpsRemaining >= 1)
            {
                Jump();
                jumpsRemaining -= 1;
            }

            rb.linearVelocityX = xVector;

// OnCollisionEnter2D — delete this method
  1. 1Ask the question first, every frame, before anything reads the answer.Update() is the frame clock, and this is a question about now. Put the same call in Start() and isGrounded is a fact about the first frame of the game, which is not what a ground check means.
  2. 3Feet down. The one branch that makes the budget rechargeable.
  3. Your turn5Put the budget back. One statement, using the two fields from the previous step: the one you spend from gets the value of the one that sets the limit. Do not write a number here — if you write = 1 you have made maxJumps a lie, and the double jump in 6.4 will not work no matter what you set it to.The field that counts down is assigned the field that holds the maximum. Same line as the one you wrote in Start(), for the same reason — one source of truth.This line is what makes the other three mean something. Without it the player jumps once per scene and then walks. A budget with no refill is not a limit, it is a one-way door.
  4. 7In the air with a full budget. Nothing has been spent, so nobody jumped — which means the player walked off the edge. Read the condition as "I am falling, and I have not used a single jump".This is the walk-off rule, and it needs no memory. You could write it with a wasGrounded field, or a timestamp, or a flag set when you jump. All of those are history, and history is another thing to keep in step. A full budget in mid-air is already the proof.
  5. 9Charge yourself one. With maxJumps at 1 this takes the budget to zero, so a player who walks off a ledge cannot then jump in mid-air. With two, it leaves one: the ground jump is gone, the air jump survives — which is what a player carrying boots expects.Why not set it to zero? Because the budget is a count, not a boolean, and this is the first line in the course that treats it as one. Charging one keeps the rule true no matter what maxJumps becomes — and maxJumps becoming 2 is the next lesson.
  6. 12The jump condition you already have. GetKeyDown is what makes one press one jump; jumpsRemaining >= 1 is the budget term — the same line, kept. What changes is that it now reads a count maintained in this loop instead of one maintained by a callback.>= 1, not > 0. They mean the same thing here, and both are correct. Pick one and be able to say why: >= 1 reads as "at least one", which is what the player is thinking.
  7. 14The method from 6.1, unchanged. The force, the ForceMode2D.Impulse, the print inside it — none of it moves today.
  8. 15Spend it, inside the if. Inside is the whole point: a jump you were not allowed to take must not cost you one.-= 1 is jumpsRemaining = jumpsRemaining - 1. It reads left to right as "take one away", which is what the player just did.
  9. 18Your horizontal movement from 6.1, untouched. It sits after every jump block on purpose — you can always walk, whether or not you have a jump.
  10. 20Take the old refill out. Once the budget is written in the frame loop, the collision callback is a second source of truth for the same number — and it is the source that is wrong about ledges. Delete the whole method. If the jump still behaves, the loop owns the budget now; if something breaks, you have just found out which line was really doing the work.Deleting it also deletes last week's answer to "what counts as ground". The tag check goes with it, and the Ground tag stops mattering to the jump entirely — that is the trade this lesson makes, and the layer is what replaces it.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Three things are worth checking. First, the refill: jumpsRemaining = maxJumps — written from the field, never from a literal. Second, the charge for walking off: one statement, in the branch that asks whether the budget is still full. Third, the order — CheckGround() runs before anything reads isGrounded, and the jump check runs after both budget rules, so one press can never be counted twice.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    // ... speed, direction, animator, renderer, cooldownTimer, rb ...

    [SerializeField] float jumpForce;          // 6.1 — the number you tuned
    bool isPlatformer = false;                 // 6.1 — set from the scene name

    [SerializeField] Transform groundCheck;    // an empty child at the feet
    [SerializeField] float groundDistance = 0.2f;
    [SerializeField] LayerMask groundMask;     // the Ground layer, and only it
    bool isGrounded;

    int jumpsRemaining;                        // how many are left right now
    int maxJumps = 1;                          // how many you get between landings

    private void Start()
    {
        // ... the component lookups and the StatManager check ...

        Scene currentScene = SceneManager.GetActiveScene();
        if (currentScene.name == "Overworld")
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 0;
            isPlatformer = false;
        }
        else
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 1;
            isPlatformer = true;
            jumpsRemaining = maxJumps;         // you start on the floor
            print(jumpsRemaining);             // an instrument — delete when it is right
        }
    }

    private void Update()
    {
        // ... input, the facing block, the sword and the bullet ...

        if (!isPlatformer)
        {
            rb.linearVelocity = new Vector2(xVector, yVector);
        }
        else
        {
            CheckGround();

            if (isGrounded)
            {
                jumpsRemaining = maxJumps;     // feet down: the budget is full
            }
            else if (jumpsRemaining == maxJumps)
            {
                jumpsRemaining -= 1;           // full budget in the air: you fell
            }

            if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.J) && jumpsRemaining >= 1)
            {
                Jump();
                jumpsRemaining -= 1;           // spend it only if you jumped
            }

            rb.linearVelocityX = xVector;
        }

        // ... cooldownTimer, the sword, the bullet, UpdateAnimation() ...
    }

    void CheckGround()
    {
        isGrounded = Physics2D.Raycast(groundCheck.position, Vector2.down, groundDistance, groundMask);
    }

    void OnDrawGizmos()
    {
        if (groundCheck == null) { return; }
        Gizmos.color = Color.red;
        Gizmos.DrawLine(groundCheck.position, groundCheck.position + Vector3.down * groundDistance);
    }

    void Jump()
    {
        print("jump");
        rb.AddForceY(jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    }
}
Build Lab: Prove It, Then Break It ~20 min

Step 1 — the five jumps. Press Play and count in each situation: on the floor (one, then nothing), landing again (one again), walking off a ledge and pressing J (nothing — the walk-off rule charged you), landing on the cave mouth (one — the layer caught it), and in mid-air over nothing after a normal jump (nothing).

Step 2 — watch the number. Keep the print() in Start() and add one to the charge for a minute. Press Play, then walk off a ledge: the Console should read the budget drop by one the frame the red line stops hitting. Take both prints out before you commit.

Step 3 — the empty mask. Set Ground Mask to Nothing and play. The red line still draws, the floor is still there, and you can jump forever — nothing errors. Put it back, and say which line of your code was right the whole time.

Step 4 — the charge that is a literal. Change jumpsRemaining -= 1; in the walk-off branch to jumpsRemaining = 0;, then later set maxJumps = 2. Walking off now costs both jumps. One of those two versions is a game rule and the other is a coincidence of today's number.

Architectural specification: the budget.
  • Where does the number of allowed jumps live, and how many places read it? A limit written into a condition is a limit nobody can tune.
  • Is the spend inside the same condition as the jump? Say what the player experiences when it is not.
  • Which surfaces count as ground, and how does the code know? Name the mechanism — a tag, a layer, a component — and one surface it gets wrong.
  • Which of the two budget rules is the refill, and which is the charge? Say what a player loses if you ship only one of them.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why a jump needs a budget rather than a rule
  • Say why maxJumps exists as a field and why the refill reads it instead of a literal
  • Explain why the decrement sits inside the if
  • Say what a raycast tells you that a collision callback cannot, and what a LayerMask is for
  • Explain why a full budget in mid-air is proof that the player walked off, with no previous frame remembered
  • Commit and push
